extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students studying discrete mathematics / introductory proof-based courses
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, properties, proof techniques, and examples about functions (as sets), injective/surjective/bijective behavior, composition, inverses, images/preimages, and the pigeonhole principle for undergraduate discrete-math or intro-proof courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function as a set (Definition 12.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f : A → B is really just a special kind of set; any function f : A → B is a subset of A × B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treating a function as a set of ordered pairs removes ambiguity of informal 'rule' descriptions and makes functions concrete mathematical objects. In practice one may think of functions as rules, but the set-theoretic definition is foundational for rigorous work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain, codomain, and range (distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Domain is the set of first coordinates (inputs), codomain is the target set B in f : A → B, and range is the set of actual outputs {f(x): x ∈ A}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful: range ⊆ codomain and surjectivity is the condition range = codomain. Exercises and examples illustrate calculating domain, codomain, and range from a list of ordered pairs or formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Two functions f : A → B and g : C → D are equal if f = g as sets (equivalently f(x) = g(x) for every x in their domain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equal functions must have equal domains. Functions may have different codomains yet be equal if they agree on every input in the (shared) domain (example: f : Z → R and g : Z → Z with same rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation for functions with product domains
rubrics_metrics.description: For f : A × A → B it is common to write f(m,n) instead of f((m,n)); similar simplifications are common elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This notation is analogous to writing f x instead of f(x); it helps readability for functions on Cartesian products. Use any reasonable symbol for functions (f,g,h or Greek letters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Injective / Surjective / Bijective (Definition 12.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Injective: for every x,y ∈ A, x ≠ y implies f(x) ≠ f(y). Surjective: for every b ∈ B there exists a ∈ A with f(a)=b. Bijective: both injective and surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative informal descriptions: injective = unequal elements of the domain map to unequal elements of the codomain; surjective = every element of the codomain has a preimage. Use these precise quantifier-based definitions in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual tests for injectivity and surjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Injective: no two domain elements point to the same codomain element. Surjective: every codomain element has at least one arrow coming to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrow diagrams (mapping diagrams) and Venn-style sketches help visualize the four possible combinations (injective/surjective or not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving a function is injective (two main approaches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct approach: assume x,y ∈ A and x ≠ y and deduce f(x) ≠ f(y). Contrapositive approach: assume f(x) = f(y) and deduce x = y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contrapositive is often easier, especially when f is given by an algebraic formula, because it starts from an equation and works toward equality of inputs. The textbook gives outlines and examples using both approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproving injectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: To show f is not injective, provide explicit x ≠ y in A with f(x) = f(y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single counterexample suffices. The text demonstrates with examples like f(x)=x^2 on R (f(2)=f(−2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving a function is surjective
rubrics_metrics.description: To show f : A → B is surjective, show ∀ b ∈ B ∃ a ∈ A with f(a)=b (often: suppose arbitrary b and construct or solve for an a depending on b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding a depends on how f is defined — solve f(a)=b for a if possible, or use common-sense constructions. The textbook gives explicit solving examples and constructive choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproving surjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: To show f is not surjective, exhibit b ∈ B such that ∀ a ∈ A, f(a) ≠ b (i.e., show a codomain element has no preimage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often showing existence of such b (e.g., a negative number for x^2 mapping from R) is straightforward; a single witness suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four injective/surjective combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: A function can be (injective & surjective) bijective, injective but not surjective, surjective but not injective, or neither.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mapping diagrams to illustrate and reason about examples in each case; the text includes illustrative figures and example functions demonstrating each type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose A and B are finite sets and f : A → B. Then: (1) if |A| > |B|, f is not injective; (2) if |A| < |B|, f is not surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the principle to make non-constructive existence arguments (e.g., two subsets with equal sum, two Texans with same hair count). Recognize many proofs using it are non-constructive but can sometimes be made constructive by explicit examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function composition (Definition 12.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given f : A → B and g : B → C (codomain of f = domain of g), the composition g ∘ f : A → C is defined by g ∘ f(x) = g(f(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with order: g ∘ f applies f first then g. Composition also makes sense if range(f) ⊆ domain(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition is not commutative
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when both g ∘ f and f ∘ g are defined, they need not be equal (g ∘ f ≠ f ∘ g in general).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples with polynomials or simple formulas illustrate the noncommutativity; compute both orders to check equality or difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associativity of composition (Theorem 12.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A → B, g : B → C, h : C → D then (h ∘ g) ∘ f = h ∘ (g ∘ f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove equality by evaluating both sides on an arbitrary x ∈ A and observing both equal h(g(f(x))).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition preserves injectivity and surjectivity (Theorem 12.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f and g are injective then g ∘ f is injective. If f and g are surjective then g ∘ f is surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs: for injectivity, g(f(x)) = g(f(y)) ⇒ f(x)=f(y) (g injective) ⇒ x=y (f injective); for surjectivity, given c ∈ C choose b ∈ B with g(b)=c (g surjective) and then a ∈ A with f(a)=b (f surjective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity function (Definition 12.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: The identity on A is i_A : A → A defined by i_A(x)=x for every x ∈ A; i_A is bijective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identity functions satisfy i_A ∘ f = f and f ∘ i_A = f when domains/codomains match appropriately; used in characterizing inverses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse relation and inverse function (Definition 12.7 & Theorem 12.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a relation R from A to B, R^{-1} = {(y,x) : (x,y) ∈ R}. For a function f, its inverse relation f^{-1} is a function iff f is bijective; in that case f^{-1} : B → A satisfies f^{-1} ∘ f = i_A and f ∘ f^{-1} = i_B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterexamples show if f is not injective or not surjective then f^{-1} fails to be a function. To compute an inverse, solve y = f(x), swap variables to get x = f(y), and solve for y to obtain f^{-1}(x) where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computing inverses (practical method)
rubrics_metrics.description: To find f^{-1}, write y = f(x), interchange variables (x ↔ y), then solve for y to express y = f^{-1}(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep track of domains/codomains and coordinates for multivariate functions; check by composing f^{-1}∘f = i_A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image and preimage (Definition 12.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f : A → B and X ⊆ A, f(X) = {f(x): x ∈ X} ⊆ B. For Y ⊆ B, f^{-1}(Y) = {x ∈ A: f(x) ∈ Y} ⊆ A. f^{-1}(Y) is defined even when f is not invertible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish f^{-1}(Y) (preimage of a set) from f^{-1}(y) (inverse function at an element, which may not exist). Note f^{-1}(f(X)) ⊇ X in general but need not equal X; f(f^{-1}(Y)) ⊆ Y in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic set-theoretic properties of images and preimages (Theorem 12.4)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are standard inclusion/equality relationships used in proofs; exercises ask to prove each item and to provide counterexamples where equality may fail.
